segments.title: HMS Coreopsis and the naval drifter Coreopsis II
segments.summary: The Flower-class sloop HMS Coreopsis was a different vessel from the drifter Coreopsis II, which took part in a destroyer-led sinking of a submarine tentatively identified as UB-85.
segments.body: HMS Coreopsis, the Flower-class sloop, should be distinguished from the naval drifter Coreopsis II. The drifter took part in a destroyer-led submarine sinking off northern Britain. The submarine is tentatively identified as UB-85. The location is also described hesitantly, with northern England corrected to somewhere near Scotland.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes the sloop HMS Coreopsis from Her Majesty's drifter Coreopsis II. It tentatively identifies the submarine in the drifter's destroyer-led sinking as UB-85 and hesitantly corrects the location from northern England towards Scotland.

segments.title: Coreopsis as a concealed-armament Q-ship
segments.summary: Coreopsis served as a decoy warship with concealed guns, operating with the Grand Fleet, in the Mediterranean, and from Gibraltar under false names.
segments.body: Coreopsis is an outstanding example of a First World War Q-ship. Concealed armament supported her employment as a decoy. She served with the Grand Fleet and in the Mediterranean, and operated from Gibraltar under the false names Bursley and Biggo. She was sold for breaking up in 1922, after a wartime career that helped define the Royal Navy's later sloop concept.

evidence.note: The transcript describes concealed-armament decoy service, Grand Fleet and Mediterranean deployments, Gibraltar false names, and sale in 1922.

segments.title: Coreopsis's dimensions and stated carrying margin
segments.summary: Coreopsis's dimensions and stated carrying margin of roughly 450 tons show the capacity of a small sloop, although the tonnage comparison is unclear.
segments.body: The tonnage comparison gives a fully laden figure of 1,760 tons alongside displacement figures of 1,200 and 1,311 tons. The distinction between the two lower figures is unclear. The carrying margin is stated as roughly 450 tons. Coreopsis measured 262 feet 3 inches overall with a 35-foot beam. Her fully laden draft could reach 13 feet 8 inches.

evidence.note: The transcript gives 1,760 tons fully laden, mentions displacement figures of 1,200 and 1,311 tons without clearly distinguishing them, and states a carrying margin of 450 tons. It then gives the overall length, beam and fully laden draft.

segments.title: Coreopsis's weapons and operating requirements
segments.summary: A top speed of 16 knots, 260 tons of coal, QF 4-inch Mark IV guns, lighter guns, depth charges, and a complement of 92 show what the small hull carried.
segments.body: Coreopsis had a top speed of 16 knots and could carry 260 tons of coal. Her armament included two quick-firing (QF) 4-inch Mark IV guns, two 12-pounder guns and depth charges. She often also carried 3-pounder guns. She was heavily armed for such a small vessel, with a complement of 92.

evidence.note: The transcript lists speed, coal, gun and depth-charge armament, and the complement.

segments.title: From Flower-class vessel to modern sloop concept
segments.summary: Coreopsis helps explain the First World War roots of the later Royal Navy sloop, even though the class was originally ordered for minesweeping rather than Q-ship duty.
segments.body: Coreopsis is an early example of the kind of sloop the Royal Navy developed after the First World War. Q-ship service was one possible use, but it was an adaptation rather than the class's original purpose. The Flower-class vessels were first ordered for minesweeping. A specialist minesweeping requirement produced ships that could later take on Q-ship and other duties.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the vessel an origin point for later sloops, notes Q-ship employment, and says the type was first ordered for minesweeping.

segments.title: Why peacetime small ships needed several roles
segments.summary: The overlap between sloops and minesweepers reflects operational utility and the political case needed to secure funding for small warships in peacetime.
segments.body: Through the 1910s, 1920s, and 1930s, sloops and minesweepers often met closely related needs. A small warship had to perform several duties instead of remaining tied to one task. Wartime construction could receive money quickly, whereas peacetime programmes needed a strong political justification. Minesweeping supplied a clear requirement, and a multi-purpose hull gave the navy broader value from the same procurement.

evidence.note: The transcript connects sloop-minesweeper overlap, multi-purpose capability, wartime funding, and the need to justify peacetime construction.
